Ground rules

If any question is answered with yes toss it

  • Does it smell weird/diffrent/funky/odd?
  • Has the color or texture changed?
  • Is the product less effective?
  • Do you break out when using the product?

Also good hygiene will prolong the shelf life while bad will shorten it severly.

Clean your brushes thoroughly, if used with any product that contains moisture clean after each use, if used with powder clean after 3 uses max! Clean brushes with soap and water the hang dry them wit the bristles facing the floor.

Switch out puffs with regular inter walls, depending on use 2-3 months is a good start. Any makeup sponges are 1 use only. That means you either clean them after each use or toss them.

Don't use your fingers in containers. Try to avoid wetting dry products. Make sure you clean any spillage on tubes, pumps etc and don't let products sit open for long periods off time. Store products cool, dry and dark if possible. Never share makeup with anyone, especially mascara or eye products. Sterilize your pencil sharpener and eyelash curler regularly, once a week is a good start.

Eyes

  • Mascara 3 months
  • Liquid eyeliner 3 months
  • Kohl pen eyeliner 1-3 years depending on how you store and how often you sharpen it
  • Gel liner/pot eyeliner 2-3 months, depending on brush cleanliness
  • Eye shadow pressed or powder around 6 months-2 year depending on how well you maintain clean brushes, if you wet the shadow it will only last 6 months
  • Creme eye shadow around 3-6 months
  • Eye shadow primer around a year depending on container, pump bottles gather less bacteria and hold for longer
  • Any powders specific for eye makeup around 1-2 years
  • Concealer liquid anywhere from 3 months to a year, wands trap more dirt than a pump bottle or tube, roll ons get contaminated as fast as a pot or creme

Face

  • Concealer around 3-6 months if it is used on pimples and rashes, pumps last up to a year
  • Powder loose or compact around 2 years if you replace puffs every 3-4 months for pressed powder
  • Powder foundation around 6-12 months if you replace puffs frequently
  • Creme or mousse foundation 3-6 months, less if you use your fingers in the container
  • Liquid foundation 6-12 months tubes have lower shelf life than pumps
  • Rouge/blush pressed or powder around 2 years with proper brush maintenance
  • Rouge/blush creme 3-6 months less if you use your fingers in the container
  • Highlighter/contour creme 3-6 months
  • Highlighter contour powder 6-12 months

Skincare products

  • Sunscreen 6 months tops the efficiency of the uv block starts to lower after 3 months
  • Face wash/mousse/cream/soap around 1 year
  • Toner around 1 year
  • Serums 6-12 months anything with vitamin C and retinol will be less efficient after a few months
  • Eye creams 12 months same with vitamin C here
  • Face creams 6-12 months depending on container, pots will gather more dirt and germs
  • Face masks single use packages up to 12 months
  • Face masks in tubes up to 12 months
  • Face masks in pots around 3 months
  • All natural no preservative/ home made face masks up to 1 week if refrigirated

Lips

  • Lipstick up to 12 months, some say 2 years
  • Lip-gloss 3-4 months, some say up to 2 years but gloss is way more prone to bacteria herds than lipstick
  • Lip pencils if sharpened and stored properly 1-2 years
  • Jumbo pens/gloss sticks and similar around 6 months
  • Any powders up to 2 years
  • Lip concealer or primer somewhere around 6-12 months depending on container and application

Rest of Body

  • Nail polish a good brand will last up to 2 years depending on storage, try to avoid direct sunlight
  • Perfume 2-10 years, if it smells weird/wrong/different toss it
  • Louffas, peeling mitts, scrubber thingies and brushes 3 months tops, all your dead skin is a feast for germs!
  • Nail clippers and such tools needs to be disinfected regularly
  • Shower gels last for about 6-12 months
  • Peelings depends on ingredients 3-6 months
  • Hard soap/soap bars if you let them dry between uses around 1-2 years
  • Files and stones for your feet, 3 months, lots of dead skin here too
  • Body lotions 3-6 months
  • Body butters 3-6 months
  • Body oils 6-12 months
  • Any dry mud powders have more or less infinite shelf life

First off, let's dispel the notion that computers aren't already fast enough to breech the sentience threshold (at least in terms of complexity). There are 100 billion neurons in the average human brain. However, the fact is you need less than half of your brain to be sentient. Here is a girl, fully sentient, only half a brain (hemispherectomy). So, we can cut that 100 billion down to 50 billion right off the bat. Much of the brain has to do with other useless things a sentient AI doesn't absolutely need for sentience, such as motor control, breathing, heart rate regulation, optical processing, etc. (Blind people are sentient, eh?) The human head isn't designed to carve out those parts you don't absolutely need, so it's hard to set an exact figure. When you slice and dice it I'm being WAY generous and saying you could be sentient with 25% of the brain (probably less than that).

The average neuron requires a cool down time, so it works at about 25Hertz. Let's round up to 30Hz (30 cycles per second) @ 25 billion neurons, That's 750 Billion cycles per second. Now, my logic for processing a neuron of my neural networks is about 10 cycles, let's go with an even 333.333... cycles per neuron on average once we factor in accessing the CPU cache to get data for the neuron to crunch. That's 750*333 GHz, so a processor that can crunch 25 trillion cycles per second.

But hang on, we forgot that Evolution is dumb and persistent. So, the human brain is badly designed. For instance: The brain has inhibitory and excitatory neurons. Sometimes two neurons will stimulate the same synapses of another neuron. One neuron of each type is used in the organic brain when you want to sometimes stimulate and sometimes inhibit stimulation. This is because two different chemical soups are required to do excitatory vs inhibitory activities.

With an artificial neuron the same "bit soup" can be positive or negative in value. The same axon pathway and neuron can transmit both excitatory (+ positive) and inhibitory (- negative) numbers. Due to the mechanics of the human organic "chemputer" there are a LOT of redundant neurons. The cybernetic version can optimize those cases out, so you could use much less artificial neurons to perform the same exact job of an organic system.

I frequently try to determine and catalog the minimum complexity levels of cybernetic systems that certain behavioral traits are able to be expressed at. For example, steering right and left to move towards a sensory stimulus takes 6 neurons in the separate polarity (organic) neuronal system, but only 4 in the dual polarity (digital) neuronal system. That's a savings of 33%. Some tasks that the organic system does, like the optical nerves' processing of light data prior to sending to the cortex can be reduced by 70% or more. Let's be generous and say we only save 1/5th the neuron cost on the upgrade to cybernetic cognition.

That means we need 20 trillion cycles per second. Many mid-range smart phones have 4 cores and can process each at a rate of 2Ghz per second. Thats a total of 8 billion cycles per second. Sections of frozen sliced brain tissue were used by other studies to create the structural information that the simulation was then based off of. To get basic error bars a comparison between input stimulus and output using living ape tissue is sometimes used. The simulation scales up from there once the error rate was within limits.

The simulation was not of an actual brain either. There was much data lost in the slicing of the tissue eradicated by the blade itself. Staining was used to highlight cells of certain types on the slides.

Today there are better non-intrusive methods which make whole brains visible via scanning by laser imaging with minimal structural damage. With this new technology you could put electrodes in the freshly dead (still active) tissue, test input / outputs, then make the tissue clear, stain the whole brain to reveal different types of neurons, then scan with a laser microscope to rebuild the 3D model in software, and chart the connective pathways. Then you can run the simulation in software to compare results to the live tissue.
